The transformation design method (TDM) is used to create invisibility cloaks by performing coordinate transformations on the wave equation.
The TDM reinterprets the effect of the coordinate transformation in the material properties of the cloaking shell.
The authors consider cloaking of both electromagnetic waves (photons) and matter waves (electrons).
For electromagnetic waves, the authors assume the polarizations suffer a phase damping with a decay rate γ when passing through the cloaking shell.
For matter waves, the authors assume the spin of the incident electron experiences a coherent coupling with a hidden spin inside the cloaking shell.
The temporal steering parameter ST2 always maintains the maximal value of 2 if the system does not interact with any ancillary systems.
The authors show that the temporal steering parameter ST2 varies with time when the incident waves pass through the cloaking shell.
The classical bound for the temporal steering inequality is 1, while quantum mechanics predicts a bound of N/2, where N is the number of measurement settings.
Using temporal steering requires fewer measurement settings (two bases) compared to full quantum state tomography (three bases).
The authors note that other methods like using classical polarized fields or detecting spin direction changes can also be used to crack cloaks.
Degradation of entanglement is another possible approach to detect quantum cloaks.
